title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
An AI system was used to create a fabricated interview between a real finance presenter and a real central bank official, depicting them endorsing a fake cryptocurrency platform. The fake article was presented as legitimate news to potential victims. This is impersonation deployed in a scam context, where the system generated false statements attributed to real people without their consent or knowledge.

The failure occurred at the point where fabricated content entered circulation without authentication. No verification system prevented the fake interview from being presented to victims as real reporting. The scammers created an entire ecosystem of supporting deceptions, including fake reviews and websites, to reinforce the false narrative. It would have taken human verification of the purported interview before the article circulated, or consumer-side checks confirming the story through official channels.

It is not established whether the AI systems used were trained or deployed with awareness they would be used for fraud, or what specific models and platforms enabled the creation and distribution of these materials.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fabricated article featuring ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock discussing a fake cryptocurrency platform called Boulder Sparhaven exemplifies a growing type of scam using artificial intelligence. The fake interview, which never occurred, depicted Bullock becoming angry about Kohler's questions regarding an unlicensed trading system. Australian Securities and Investments Commission research shows that deepfake and AI-generated investment scams are increasing and becoming more sophisticated, with scammers creating elaborate webs of deception including fake news articles, reviews, and websites.

ASIC removed 19,400 scams last year, representing a 182 percent increase, with phishing scams jumping 279 percent and fake investment platforms rising 151 percent. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese tops the list of commonly impersonated Australians, followed by politicians and prominent financial figures including Alan Kohler, who has previously experienced similar AI scams. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing and warns that professional-looking content does not guarantee legitimacy. Kohler advocates for stricter penalties against platforms and AI models enabling these scams.
